Meanwhile the database cache keeps recent query results close to applications, so they avoid repeating expensive disk reads. Teams often place each cache between services and storage, which reduces latency during busy hours and protects primary databases from heavy traffic.

However this cache also introduces risks; stale values can linger after underlying rows change, so teams must define clear invalidation rules. Common strategies include time-to-live settings, write-through updates, and explicit purges when important records change; each approach trades freshness against operational complexity for every cache layer in production. Engineers should always measure hit rates carefully.

Along with that a small staff can run analytics on daily stock, pricing, and logins without much risk. All hit counts and scan totals stay in a log, which also shows what slows things and bursts in traffic.

Finally measure each cache with real traffic; numbers reveal whether caching helps, so act on evidence. Your tuning is done.
